Renal and Genitourinary Disorders

Urinary Tract Infections and Hematuria

This chapter separates lower UTI, upper UTI, complicated UTI, recurrent infection, and hematuria risk. The ED task is to identify who can receive simple outpatient therapy and who needs cultures, imaging, source control, admission, or malignancy follow-up.

Board trap: A positive UA is not the diagnosis; symptoms, host risk, catheter status, pregnancy, obstruction, sepsis, and hematuria risk factors decide treatment and disposition.

URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS

UTI is common in ED adults, especially women, older patients, and patients with urinary obstruction or instrumentation. Severity depends on anatomic level, organism, host risk, and whether the infection is uncomplicated or complicated.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND DEFINITIONS

UTI usually starts when enteric flora colonize the periurethral area and ascend. Diagnostic thresholds vary by collection method and syndrome; symptomatic women may have clinically important infection below classic 105 CFU/mL thresholds.

ASYMPTOMATIC BACTERIURIA

Asymptomatic bacteriuria is bacteriuria without UTI symptoms. Treat only pregnancy and patients immediately before invasive urologic procedures with mucosal bleeding. Treating routine bacteriuria in older or catheterized patients promotes resistance without benefit.

URETHRITIS AND CYSTITIS

Cystitis is infection isolated to the bladder with dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, and sometimes hematuria. Urethritis produces dysuria or discharge and should trigger STI consideration, especially with vaginal discharge, irritation, new partner, or urethral discharge.

PYELONEPHRITIS

Pyelonephritis involves renal parenchyma and the collecting system. Fever, chills, flank pain, CVA tenderness, nausea, vomiting, or prostration should shift thinking from simple cystitis to upper tract disease. Acute bacterial nephritis, renal abscess, and emphysematous pyelonephritis are dangerous mimics when response is atypical.

UNCOMPLICATED URINARY TRACT INFECTION

Uncomplicated UTI means a nonpregnant patient with normal anatomy and function, no major comorbidity, and no recent instrumentation. Pyelonephritis can be uncomplicated by host definition, but treatment is still more intensive than lower cystitis.

COMPLICATED URINARY TRACT INFECTION

Complicated UTI involves abnormal anatomy/function or comorbidities that raise treatment failure or adverse outcome risk. Male UTI, pregnancy, diabetes, obstruction, stones, catheter/stent, neurogenic bladder, renal transplant, immunocompromise, and recent instrumentation all matter.

RECURRENT URINARY TRACT INFECTION

Recurrent UTI means two uncomplicated UTIs in 6 months or three in 12 months. Relapse within 2 weeks by the same organism suggests a persistent urinary focus; reinfection after treatment suggests a new event.

MICROBIOLOGY

E. coli dominates uncomplicated infections; complicated and catheter-associated infections broaden to Proteus, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus, Candida, and polymicrobial biofilm. Organism expectations change empiric therapy and the need for culture.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Symptoms vary by site and host. Classic lower symptoms can be absent in older, immunocompromised, spinal cord injury, or catheterized patients, so systemic change may be the clue.

URETHRITIS

Male dysuria with urethral discharge is urethritis until proven otherwise. In women, dysuria with new sexual partner, partner with urethritis, vaginal discharge/irritation, or cervical motion tenderness points away from isolated cystitis.

CYSTITIS

Cystitis causes frequency, urgency, hesitancy, suprapubic pain/tenderness, and gross hematuria. Fever and chills are uncommon; their presence should prompt upper tract or systemic evaluation.

PYELONEPHRITIS

Pyelonephritis may present with or without lower tract symptoms. Missing cystitis is usually not catastrophic; missing pyelonephritis can become untreated sepsis.

SEPSIS FROM URINARY TRACT INFECTION

Genitourinary infection is a common sepsis source. Patients may lack typical cystitis or flank pain, especially if older or catheterized, so apply sepsis evaluation and early resuscitation/source control.

COMPLICATED URINARY TRACT INFECTION

Complicated UTI can present as fever, rigors, flank pain, altered mental status, malaise, pelvic discomfort, hematuria, catheter obstruction, spasticity, or autonomic dysreflexia in spinal cord injury.

DIAGNOSIS

A clinical diagnosis starts treatment in many patients, but cultures and imaging become more important as risk rises. A clean-catch specimen is useful when the patient can follow instructions; catheterized specimens help when voiding is not possible or contamination is likely.

URINALYSIS

Urinalysis supports the diagnosis but does not replace clinical judgment. Reference values depend on specimen type, centrifugation, and collection method.

NITRITE REACTION BY DIPSTICK TEST

Nitrite positivity is specific for organisms that reduce nitrate, but false negatives occur with non-nitrite-producing organisms and frequent voiding. A negative nitrite does not exclude UTI.

LEUKOCYTE ESTERASE REACTION BY DIPSTICK TEST

Leukocyte esterase reflects WBC enzyme activity. It supports UTI when symptoms fit, but false positives and false negatives occur; use it with symptoms, nitrite, microscopy, and risk group.

URINE WBC COUNT OR PYURIA BY MICROSCOPY

Pyuria supports inflammation, but sterile pyuria can occur with STI, stones, tuberculosis, interstitial nephritis, or partially treated infection. Absence of pyuria lowers probability but does not fully exclude complicated infection.

BACTERIURIA BY MICROSCOPY

Bacteria on microscopy may represent infection or contamination. In catheterized patients, biofilm makes bacteriuria common and symptoms determine treatment.

COMBINED RESULTS OF DIPSTICK TESTING, URINE CELL COUNTS, AND HISTORICAL INFORMATION

No single history element or dipstick result rules in or rules out all UTI. Dysuria plus frequency without vaginal symptoms has high probability; negative dipstick in low-risk patients lowers probability, but ED follow-up and culture matter when risk is higher.

URINE AND BLOOD CULTURE

Culture complicated UTI, pyelonephritis, sepsis, recurrence/relapse, recent antibiotic exposure, pregnancy, and cases where follow-up matters. Blood cultures are mainly useful when clinical sepsis is present.

IMAGING

Do not image routine uncomplicated UTI. Image severe illness, treatment failure, obstruction/stone concern, renal insufficiency, male/elderly/diabetic patients with concerning features, or suspected renal abscess/emphysematous pyelonephritis. CT is best for stone or intrarenal gas; ultrasound is useful in pregnancy or obstruction screening.

TREATMENT

Treatment follows syndrome and host risk: lower uncomplicated disease, upper/complicated disease, or urethritis overlap. Antibiotic choice must reflect local resistance and allergies.

ACUTE CYSTITIS AND UNCOMPLICATED URINARY TRACT INFECTION

Use nitrofurantoin, TMP-SMX when resistance is acceptable, or fosfomycin. Fluoroquinolones are effective but are not preferred first-line for simple cystitis because of adverse effects and resistance stewardship. If urethritis cannot be excluded, cover/evaluate STI and add cystitis treatment or culture and tailor.

ACUTE PYELONEPHRITIS AND COMPLICATED URINARY TRACT INFECTION

Stable patients may be treated as outpatients when they tolerate oral medications and follow-up is reliable. Inpatient care uses parenteral gram-negative coverage, fluids, electrolyte correction, culture-directed step-down, and source control. Replace or remove urinary catheters when feasible before cultures and antibiotics.

RECURRENT INFECTION

Reinfection can often use uncomplicated cystitis regimens. Relapse needs a complicated-UTI approach and evaluation for stones, abscess, anatomic abnormality, or persistent source. Prophylaxis belongs to outpatient follow-up, not reflex ED prescribing.

DISPOSITION AND FOLLOW-UP

Discharge healthy cystitis patients and selected stable pyelonephritis patients who tolerate fluids/meds and have return precautions. Admit sepsis, hemodynamic instability, obstruction/stone with infection, renal failure, severe pain, persistent vomiting, pregnancy with pyelonephritis, immunocompromise, unreliable follow-up, or failed outpatient therapy.

SPECIAL POPULATIONS

PREGNANCY

Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria and simple cystitis in pregnancy to prevent pyelonephritis and pregnancy complications. Avoid fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines; nitrofurantoin and TMP-SMX have trimester cautions and do not treat pyelonephritis because they do not achieve renal parenchymal levels.

PATIENTS WITH HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS INFECTION/ACQUIRED IMMUNODEFICIENCY SYNDROME

HIV patients may have typical bacterial UTI, STI mimics, opportunistic disease, renal disease, or medication complications. Culture, assess immune status, and avoid dismissing atypical symptoms as simple cystitis.

HEMATURIA

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

Gross hematuria is visible blood; microscopic hematuria is laboratory-defined RBCs. UTI is common when hematuria appears with urgency/dysuria, but painless hematuria, older age, smoking, occupational exposure, anticoagulation, or recurrent episodes require follow-up for significant disease.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Bleeding may arise anywhere from glomerulus to urethra. False hematuria occurs when urine looks red without RBCs, such as myoglobin, hemoglobin, porphyrins, foods, dyes, or intentional contamination.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Initial hematuria suggests urethral/prostatic source; terminal hematuria suggests bladder neck/trigone; total hematuria suggests upper tract or bladder. Clots generally point to nonglomerular bleeding. Hypertension, edema, casts, or proteinuria suggest renal parenchymal disease.

DIAGNOSIS

LABORATORY TESTING

Confirm dipstick blood with microscopy when the cause is not obvious. Check pregnancy test, renal function, CBC, coagulation studies, culture, or CK when suggested by presentation. Catheter specimens help women with vaginal bleeding but catheterization itself may cause hematuria.

IMAGING

Stable patients often receive outpatient urology-directed evaluation. CT or ultrasound is used when obstruction, stone, tumor, trauma, AAA, pregnancy, renal insufficiency, or severe symptoms guide the test choice. Gross hematuria after trauma needs imaging for source and management planning.

TREATMENT, DISPOSITION, AND FOLLOW-UP

Treat the cause. Gross hematuria with clots can obstruct bladder outflow and may need large-bore three-way catheter, irrigation, and urology. Admit unstable patients, obstruction/clot retention, renal failure, severe pain, PO intolerance, sepsis, or unclear life-threatening cause. Microscopic hematuria without benign explanation needs follow-up based on risk factors.
